newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW - Fernz sees positive CFPI contrib in 1998.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Fernz sees positive CFPI contrib in 1998.

text.p: Fernz Corporation's 1998 year profit will include a favourable contribution from French chemicals firm CFPI, chief executive Kerry Hoggard said on Monday.
But the complexity of the CFPI acquisition, which is not yet complete, made it difficult for Fernz to quantify CFPI's impact on the bottomline, he said.
"It will have a positive impact in the 1998 year, but it's difficult for us to quantify exactly what that's going to be at this moment in time," Hoggard told Reuters.
"There are a number of complications that result around the CFPI acquisition that will make the normal forecasts at this time of the year a bit more difficult for us."
Fernz is due to report its results for the year to May 1997 on Wednesday, and the company normally issues comprehensive profit forecasts for subsequent years at its annual meeting in October.
Fernz owns 45.14 percent of CFPI but French pharmaceuticals giant Rhone Poulenc has agreed to part with its 32 percent stake in the strategically valuable company as part of an intricate deal.
Hoggard said Fernz aimed to eventually take 100 percent of CFPI, privatise the company and sell part of it back to Rhone, but there were a multitude of small shareholders to win over first.

"But we have said all along that in the 1999 year we would expect the CFPI operation on a restructured basis to deliver positive economic value to Fernz. By implication that means it's got to do better than about NZ$16 million even," Hoggard said.

Analysts expect Fernz to post a net profit of between NZ$45.5 and $46 million for the 1997 year, up only slightly from last year's $43.5 million and below the company's own forecast of $47.3 million. Fernz previously forecast a $58.7 million 1998 profit.

Hoggard conceded that some of Fernz's existing businesses were mature, with growth rates of only four to five percent per annum, but he said recent acquisitions would boost growth rates for the group.
He said Fernz and Rhone planned to form a joint venture company to market the agricultural herbicides on which the two have a world stranglehold -- Bromoxynil and MCPA.

"What we've endeavoured to do in our European operations, which have gone extremely well for us, is to try and find chemicals which have got niche markets where there isn't too much competition," Hoggard said.
"We've got a half a billion dollar business in agricultural chemicals, so it's a big part of our operation."
Hoggard said Fernz had made several international acquisitions in the chemicals industry over the past three years as it refocused on the agricultural and industrial chemicals industry.
"We've been very active in the ag-chem and industrial market over the last three years, with major acquisitions in the UK, Austria, Holland, and in Australasia.

"We've recently put a lot of development emphasis into our industrial chemicals business, which has also grown very significantly and has this year gone from $70 million turnover to $250 million turnover," he said.
"So we have been very active and will continue to be."
Earlier this year Fernz exited the fertiliser business, from where its name, Fertiliser Company of New Zealand, originates.
But Hoggard said changing the company's name was not on the agenda.
"No. The name Fernz is now well recognised in the commercial markets -- there's absolutely no reason to change it -- it could mean anything," he said.
